title: How Capital Gains Taxes Work When You Sell a Home
bigPicture: When you sell your main home for more than you paid, you may be able to leave up to $250,000 of the profit out of your income ($500,000 if you file a joint return), if you owned it and lived in it for at least 2 of the last 5 years.
whatYouNeedToKnow: A capital gain is the profit on a sale, not the whole sale price.
The IRS lets you exclude up to $250,000 of gain, or up to $500,000 if you file a joint return with your spouse.
You must have owned the home and used it as your main home for at least 2 years (24 months) out of the 5 years before the sale. The two 2-year periods do not have to be the same.
On a joint return, either spouse can meet the ownership test, but both spouses must meet the use test.
The exclusion only applies to your main home.
The cost of additions and improvements is added to your home's cost basis, which lowers your gain.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Throwing away receipts for big improvements. They raise your cost basis.
Assuming every sale is tax-free. The 2-of-5-year ownership and use tests must be met.

Skipping the report because you think you owe nothing. If you receive Form 1099-S you must report the sale, even if the gain can be excluded. You must also report it if you cannot exclude all of the gain.
Expecting the same exclusion on a second home. It only applies to your main home.
actionSteps: Gather the receipts for additions and improvements you have made.
Write down what you paid for the home plus those improvement costs. That is your adjusted cost basis.
Subtract your adjusted basis from the sale price to estimate your gain.
Check that you meet both the ownership test and the use test for 2 of the last 5 years.
Read the IRS pages listed below, or ask a tax preparer, before you file.
